short: The formal Muslim prayer, performed five times a day at set times, facing Makkah.
long: The word means connection and supplication. Salah is a fixed sequence of standing, bowing, prostrating and sitting, with recitation from the Qur'an, done at five appointed times between dawn and night. It is the second pillar of Islam and the first act a person is asked about on the Day of Judgement. Persian and Urdu speakers usually call it namaz, which is the same thing.

short: The five obligatory prayers: dawn, past midday, afternoon, just after sunset, and night.
long: Fajr runs from true dawn until sunrise. Dhuhr begins once the sun has passed its highest point. Asr fills the later afternoon, Maghrib begins at sunset, and Isha begins once the twilight has gone and lasts until dawn. The schools differ over exactly when Asr begins, and over which twilight closes the time of Maghrib, which is why mosques in the same city sometimes call these times an hour apart.

short: One complete unit of prayer: a standing, a bowing, and two prostrations.
long: Prayers are counted in rak'ahs. Fajr is two, Maghrib is three, and Dhuhr, Asr and Isha are four each. Within one rak'ah you stand and recite, bow, rise, prostrate, sit, and prostrate again. The plural is raka'at, which is why you will hear both forms.

short: The standing part of the prayer, where al-Fatihah and other verses are recited.
long: Qiyam simply means standing. Standing is required in obligatory prayers for anyone able to do it; someone who cannot stand prays sitting, and someone who cannot sit prays lying down, with no loss of reward. The same word appears in qiyam al-layl, meaning standing in prayer through the night.

short: The bowing in prayer, hands on the knees, back level, praising Allah's greatness.
long: From the standing position you bow with the back straight and the hands resting on the knees, saying subhana rabbiyal azim, glory to my Lord the Magnificent. The Qur'an repeatedly commands the believers to bow, and the posture is one of the pillars of the prayer without which a rak'ah does not count.

short: The prostration, forehead and nose on the ground, done twice in every rak'ah.
long: Seven parts touch the ground: the forehead with the nose, the two palms, the two knees, and the toes of both feet. The Prophet said a servant is nearest to his Lord in sujud, and told us to make much supplication there. It is the posture the whole prayer is built around, not a formality between recitations.

short: The words said while sitting in prayer, testifying to faith and greeting the Prophet.
long: The name comes from shahadah, testimony, because the words contain the declaration of faith. It is said in the sitting after the second rak'ah and again at the end of the prayer, where salawat on the Prophet is added before the closing salam. Several wordings are authentically reported, and mosques in different regions use different ones; all of them are sound.

short: The closing greeting of peace, turned to the right then the left, that ends the prayer.
long: You say as-salamu alaykum wa rahmatullah while turning the face to the right shoulder, then repeat it to the left. Until the taslim you are still in prayer and its restrictions apply. Some schools treat only the first salam as obligatory and the second as recommended.

short: The opening "Allahu akbar" that begins the prayer and closes off everything outside it.
long: Ihram here means entering a sanctified state, the same root as the pilgrim's ihram. Once you say the opening takbir, eating, speaking and turning away are no longer permitted until the closing salam. Smaller takbirs then mark each change of posture through the prayer.

short: The intention in the heart that turns an ordinary act into an act of worship.
long: Every act of worship needs a niyyah, and the Prophet said actions are only by intentions. It lives in the heart, so knowing which prayer you have stood up for is already the intention. The schools differ over whether saying it aloud helps: Shafi'is and Hanbalis allow it as an aid to focus, Malikis prefer it left unsaid, and none of them count the spoken words as the intention itself.

short: Stillness of the body and attention of the heart during prayer.
long: The Qur'an opens its description of successful believers with those who have khushu' in their prayer. It is not an emotion you must manufacture; it is mainly the practice of returning your attention each time it wanders, and of not fidgeting. Losing focus does not invalidate the prayer, which is why nobody should stop praying out of a feeling that their prayer is not good enough.

short: A supplication said standing in prayer, most often in witr or in times of crisis.
long: The word means devout standing. The schools place it differently: Hanafis say it in witr all year, Shafi'is in the dawn prayer and in witr in the second half of Ramadan, Malikis in the dawn prayer, and Hanbalis in witr. Most also recognise qunut an-nazilah, a supplication added during public calamity. Its wording is not fixed, so a person may ask in their own words.

short: An odd-numbered night prayer, usually one or three rak'ahs, that closes the night.
long: Witr means odd, as opposed to even. It is prayed any time after Isha until dawn, and the Prophet told his companions to make it the last prayer of their night. Hanafis classify it as wajib, close to obligatory; the other three schools call it a confirmed sunnah. Someone who intends to pray tahajjud usually delays witr until after it.

short: Voluntary prayer in the night, traditionally after sleeping and before dawn.
long: The root means to give up sleep. The Qur'an addresses the Prophet directly about it, and the last third of the night is its best time. There is no fixed number of rak'ahs; two is enough. Qiyam al-layl is a broader term for any prayer of the night, and in ordinary use the two words are treated as the same thing.

short: A voluntary prayer of two to eight rak'ahs in the mid-morning, after sunrise and before noon.
long: Its time opens once the sun has risen clearly above the horizon and closes shortly before midday. The Prophet described a charity due from every joint in the body each morning, and said two rak'ahs of duha are enough for all of it. Some call the earliest part of that window ishraq, and in the subcontinent it is often called chasht.

short: The night prayer of Ramadan, prayed in congregation after Isha through the month.
long: The name comes from the pauses for rest taken after every four rak'ahs. The number differs by custom and school: twenty rak'ahs became the settled practice of most schools and thirty six the old practice of Madinah, while many mosques pray eight, following reports of the Prophet's own night prayer. The number is not the point of the argument it is often made into; both are within the tradition.

short: The regular voluntary prayers attached before or after the five obligatory ones.
long: Twelve rak'ahs are reported as the standing pattern: two before Fajr, four before and two after Dhuhr, two after Maghrib, and two after Isha. The two before Fajr were the ones the Prophet never left. Any voluntary prayer outside this pattern is called nafl, and it carries no blame if missed.

short: The Friday congregational prayer: a sermon followed by two rak'ahs, replacing Dhuhr.
long: The Qur'an commands believers to leave off trade and hurry to the remembrance of Allah when the Friday call is made. It is obligatory on adult resident men who are able to attend, and not obligatory on women, travellers or the sick, though all may attend. Whoever misses it prays Dhuhr as normal.

short: The sermon given before the Friday prayer and after the two Eid prayers.
long: The Friday khutbah comes in two parts with a brief sitting between them, and it is delivered before the prayer, not after. Scholars explain it as standing in place of two of the four Dhuhr rak'ahs, so listening to it is part of the worship, and most hold that talking while it is delivered is forbidden. The Eid khutbah works the other way round: it follows the prayer, and staying for it is recommended rather than required.

short: The two rak'ah prayer on the morning of the two Eids, with extra takbirs and a sermon after.
long: It is prayed in the mid-morning, in congregation, without adhan or iqamah, and the number of added takbirs differs by school. Rulings on it differ too: Hanafis call it wajib, Hanbalis a communal obligation, Shafi'is and Malikis a confirmed sunnah. Praying it in an open space rather than inside the mosque is the older practice.

short: The funeral prayer, said standing over the deceased, with no bowing and no prostration.
long: It consists of four takbirs said while standing: al-Fatihah in the Shafi'i and Hanbali schools and praise of Allah in the Hanafi and Maliki, then salawat on the Prophet, then supplication for the deceased, then the closing salam. It is a communal obligation, meaning that if enough people pray it the duty is lifted from the rest. It is a prayer for the dead person, not a ceremony for the family, which is why it is kept short.

short: Two voluntary rak'ahs followed by a supplication asking Allah to choose the better of two paths.
long: The word means asking for the good. The Prophet taught it for ordinary decisions, and it is prayed once you already have an inclination, not instead of thinking and asking advice. A common misunderstanding is that it must produce a dream or a sign; it does not. You pray, you decide, and you trust the outcome you are given.

short: Shortening the four-rak'ah prayers to two while travelling, and combining two prayers in one time.
long: The Qur'an mentions shortening prayer on a journey, and the Prophet did it consistently. Qasr applies to Dhuhr, Asr and Isha only; Fajr and Maghrib are never shortened. Jam' is a separate concession, joining Dhuhr with Asr or Maghrib with Isha. The schools set different thresholds for how far you must travel and how long you may stay before you pray in full again.

short: Praying together behind one imam, which multiplies the reward of the prayer many times over.
long: The Prophet said congregational prayer surpasses praying alone by twenty seven degrees. Two people are enough to form a jama'ah. The schools differ on how binding it is for men: Hanbalis hold it individually obligatory, Shafi'is a communal obligation, and Hanafis and Malikis a confirmed sunnah. Someone who joins late catches up alone after the imam finishes.

short: The person who leads the prayer, standing in front while the rows follow his movements.
long: The word means one who is in front. The Prophet said the person who leads should be the one who knows most Qur'an, then the most learned in the sunnah. Any competent adult man can lead; it is not a clerical office or a job title, and most mosques employ one only for convenience. In wider usage imam also names a great scholar, as in Imam Malik, and in Shia Islam it carries a specific and much larger meaning.

short: The call announcing that a prayer time has entered, given aloud before each obligatory prayer.
long: It was taught to the companions in Madinah after they discussed how to gather people, and Bilal was its first caller. Its lines declare Allah's greatness, the testimony of faith, and the summons to prayer and to success. The Fajr adhan adds the line that prayer is better than sleep. The one who calls it is the muezzin.

short: The second, shorter call given immediately before the congregation starts the prayer.
long: Its words are almost those of the adhan, with the added line qad qamat as-salah, the prayer has begun. Hanafis repeat its phrases as in the adhan; the other three schools say most of them once. It is also given, quietly, by a person praying alone, and the schools differ over how binding it is.

short: The direction of the Kaaba in Makkah, which Muslims face when they pray.
long: For sixteen or seventeen months in Madinah the Muslims prayed towards Jerusalem, and in the second year after the hijrah the Qur'an turned them to the Sacred Mosque. Those far from Makkah are asked for the direction rather than a perfect line, and someone with no way of knowing prays towards their best judgement and the prayer counts. Mosques mark it with a niche called the mihrab.

short: Two extra prostrations that repair a mistake made by forgetting during the prayer.
long: They cover adding a posture, leaving out a required part, or losing count. The Prophet said that when a person is unsure, he should settle on the lower number and make the two prostrations. The schools place them differently, before or after the closing salam depending on the kind of mistake, so follow what your local imam does rather than assuming an error.

short: A single prostration made when reciting or hearing one of the Qur'an's verses of prostration.
long: Copies of the Qur'an mark these verses in the margin. Depending on the school they are counted as eleven, fourteen or fifteen. It is one prostration, done inside or outside prayer, and it is recommended rather than required for most scholars. A related act is sujud ash-shukr, a prostration of thanks on receiving good news.

short: Performing an obligatory act of worship after its proper time has passed, to make it up.
long: The Qur'an tells whoever is ill or travelling in Ramadan to fast the same number of other days, which is the clearest case of qada. Missed prayers are made up as soon as one is able, in order where practical, and there is no need to announce or dramatise it. Someone with years of missed prayers is usually advised to add a few to each day rather than attempt to clear them at once.

short: Ritual purity, the state a person must be in before praying and, for most scholars, before touching the Qur'an.
long: Books of fiqh almost always begin with taharah, because it is the gate to everything else. It has two sides: removing physical filth from the body, clothes and place of prayer, and lifting the ritual states that block worship. The Prophet called purification half of faith, and the Qur'an says Allah loves those who keep themselves pure.

short: The washing done before prayer: face, arms to the elbows, wiping the head, and feet to the ankles.
long: The four acts are named directly in the Qur'an, and the Prophet added rinsing the mouth and nose, washing the hands first, and doing each part three times. Wudu is broken by using the toilet, by passing wind, and by deep sleep; it is not broken by touching an animal or by ordinary dirt. One wudu lasts for as many prayers as you like until something breaks it.

short: The full washing of the whole body that lifts the major state of ritual impurity.
long: It is required after intercourse or sexual discharge, and at the end of menstruation and postnatal bleeding. It is recommended before Jumu'ah, the two Eids, and entering ihram. At minimum it is an intention and water reaching every part of the skin and hair; the schools differ over whether rinsing the mouth and nose, and rubbing the skin, are obligatory or recommended. A ghusl done properly also counts for wudu.

short: Purification with clean earth instead of water, when water is unavailable or would cause harm.
long: You strike clean ground or dust with the palms and wipe the face and the hands. The Qur'an permits it for the traveller, the ill, and anyone who cannot find water. It stands in for both wudu and ghusl, and it ends the moment water becomes usable again. It is a real concession, not a lesser or shameful substitute.

short: A substance counted as ritually impure, which must be removed from body, clothes and prayer place.
long: Urine, faeces, blood, pork and wine are the agreed cases. Water removes najasah once the colour, taste and smell are gone. The schools differ over particular cases, such as dogs, and over how small a trace is overlooked. Najasah is about the substance; the state of a person needing wudu or ghusl is hadath, and the two are often confused.

short: The ritual state that blocks prayer until it is lifted by wudu or by ghusl.
long: Minor hadath comes from things like using the toilet or sleeping deeply, and is lifted by wudu. Major hadath comes from sexual discharge, menstruation and postnatal bleeding, and is lifted by ghusl. It is a legal state, not dirt: a person in hadath may be perfectly clean, and a person covered in mud may have valid wudu.

short: The state following intercourse or sexual discharge, lifted only by a full ghusl.
long: A person in this state is called junub. Until they wash, prayer and tawaf are not performed and, for most scholars, the Qur'an is not recited or carried. The Qur'an mentions it plainly alongside the verse on wudu, and there is nothing shameful in it; it is simply a state with a known remedy. If water is unavailable, tayammum stands in for the ghusl.

short: Menstruation, during which prayer and fasting are lifted and intimacy is paused.
long: Prayers missed in these days are not made up, but fasts of Ramadan are. Nifas is the parallel state of bleeding after childbirth and carries the same rulings. Bleeding outside these two, called istihadah, does not excuse prayer or fasting. The schools differ over the minimum and maximum days of hayd, which changes when a woman resumes worship, so local guidance matters here.

short: Wiping over footwear in wudu instead of washing the feet, once they were put on in purity.
long: The permission is very widely reported from the Prophet. It lasts one day and night for a resident and three days and nights for a traveller, counted from the first wipe after wudu was broken. It ends with ghusl or with taking the socks off. Whether ordinary cotton socks qualify or only thick leather ones is an old and continuing discussion among scholars.

short: A twig used to clean the teeth, recommended before prayer, wudu, and on waking.
long: It is cut from the arak tree, softened at one end into bristles. The Prophet said that were it not a hardship, he would have ordered it before every prayer. It is a sunnah of cleanliness rather than a condition of anything, and a toothbrush achieves most of the same purpose for anyone who has no arak wood.

short: Fasting: abstaining from food, drink and intimacy from true dawn until sunset, with intention.
long: The word means to hold back. Fasting the month of Ramadan is the fourth pillar, and voluntary fasts are kept on other days through the year. The Qur'an sets its purpose as taqwa, God consciousness, and the Prophet warned that a fast without leaving off false speech is only hunger and thirst. Illness, travel, pregnancy, nursing, menstruation and old age all carry recognised concessions.

short: The meal eaten before dawn to begin a day of fasting.
long: The name comes from sahar, the last darkness before dawn. The Prophet said to eat it because there is blessing in it, and encouraged delaying it until close to the dawn. It is a sunnah rather than a condition, so a fast is still valid if a person sleeps through it.

short: Breaking the fast at sunset, traditionally with dates and water before the Maghrib prayer.
long: The Prophet hastened it rather than delaying it, and said people remain in good as long as they do so. He broke his fast with fresh dates, or dry dates, or else a drink of water. Feeding a fasting person their iftar is described as earning the same reward as their fast, which is the origin of the communal iftar tables.

short: Staying in a mosque for a set period, devoted to worship and cut off from ordinary business.
long: The word means to keep to something. The Qur'an mentions it in the verses on fasting, and the Prophet kept i'tikaf in the last ten nights of Ramadan every year. The one in retreat leaves only for necessity. Hanafis allow a woman to observe it in the place she prays at home; the other schools hold that it must be in a mosque.

short: A fixed expiation owed for certain deliberate breaches, heavier than simply making the act up.
long: For deliberately breaking a Ramadan fast, the expiation is to fast sixty consecutive days, or if unable, to feed sixty poor people, alongside making up the day. Hanafis and Malikis apply this to deliberate eating and drinking as well as intercourse; Shafi'is and Hanbalis restrict it to intercourse. A separate and much lighter kaffarah exists for breaking an oath. It is not owed by someone who broke the fast by mistake or out of genuine need.

short: Feeding a poor person for each fast that a person is permanently unable to keep or make up.
long: The Qur'an mentions it for those who can only fast with great hardship, which scholars apply to the very old and the chronically ill with no prospect of recovery. It is one meal or its value for each missed day, given to someone in need. Anyone who expects to recover owes qada instead, and should not pay fidyah to avoid fasting.

short: The yearly obligatory share of qualifying wealth, normally 2.5 percent, given to those entitled to it.
long: The word carries both purification and growth. Zakat is the third pillar, and the Qur'an names it beside the prayer again and again. It is due on savings, gold, silver and trade goods held for a lunar year above the nisab, at one fortieth of their value, while crops, livestock and mined wealth have their own rates. It is a debt owed to specific people, not a donation the giver may direct wherever they wish.

short: The minimum amount of wealth a person must hold before zakat becomes due on it.
long: It is set by the Prophet's rulings at about 85 grams of gold or about 595 grams of silver, with slightly different weights reported. Scholars differ over which standard to apply to cash: the silver figure is much lower, so it brings more people into zakat and gives more to the poor, while the gold figure sets a higher threshold and is widely used today. Below the nisab, no zakat is owed and nothing is blameworthy.

short: The full lunar year that wealth must be held above the nisab before zakat falls due on it.
long: You set a date, usually a day in Ramadan for ease of memory, and pay on whatever qualifying wealth you hold on that date each year. Hanafis fold money that comes and goes during the year into that one date; the other schools start a fresh year for wealth newly acquired. Crops are the exception: their zakat is due at harvest, and buried treasure is due at once.

short: A small measure of staple food given for every household member before the Eid al-Fitr prayer.
long: The Prophet made it obligatory on every Muslim, young and old, free and owned, as a purification for the fasting person and food for the poor. The measure is one sa', roughly two and a half to three kilograms of the local staple. Hanafis permit paying its value in money, which most charities now do; the other schools generally require the food itself. Given after the Eid prayer it counts as ordinary charity, so it is paid early.

short: Voluntary giving, of any amount and at any time, to anyone in need.
long: The root is sidq, truthfulness, because giving is treated as proof that a claim to faith is real. Unlike zakat it has no threshold, no fixed rate and no fixed recipients. The Prophet counted removing harm from a path, a good word, and a smile as sadaqah, so it is not limited to money. Giving quietly is described in the Qur'an as better than giving openly.

short: A charity that keeps benefiting people, so its reward continues after the giver dies.
long: Jariyah means flowing. The Prophet said that when a person dies their deeds stop except for three, and named ongoing charity, knowledge that others benefit from, and a righteous child who prays for them. A well, a tree, a school and a copy of the Qur'an left for others are the classic examples. Endowing property permanently for this purpose is called waqf.

short: The eight groups the Qur'an names as the only lawful recipients of zakat.
long: They are the poor, the needy, those employed to collect it, those whose hearts are to be reconciled, freeing those in bondage, the debt burdened, the cause of Allah, and the stranded traveller. The list is fixed by a single verse, which is why most scholars hold that zakat cannot be spent on a mosque building or a general good cause the way sadaqah can. Scholars differ over how widely the seventh category may be read.

short: A fifth of certain wealth; in Sunni law on spoils and treasure, in Shia practice a yearly payment.
long: The Qur'an assigns a fifth of the spoils of war to named recipients, and Sunni schools extend this to rikaz, wealth found buried in the ground. Twelver Shia jurisprudence reads the verse far more broadly, as a fifth of a person's yearly surplus income, paid through a marja' and divided between the share of the Imam and the descendants of the Prophet. A reader meeting the word in a Shia context is meeting this second meaning.

short: The pilgrimage to Makkah in Dhul Hijjah, obligatory once in a lifetime on those who are able.
long: It is the fifth pillar. The condition of ability, called istita'ah, covers health, safe passage and the money to travel and to leave dependants provided for; someone who lacks these owes nothing. The rites run over several days across Makkah, Mina, Arafah and Muzdalifah, retracing the acts of Ibrahim, Hajar and Isma'il. Umrah can be done at any time of year, but hajj cannot.

short: The lesser pilgrimage: ihram, tawaf, sa'i and cutting the hair, and it may be done any time of year.
long: It shares its rites with hajj but has no Arafah, no Mina and no fixed date. It takes a few hours rather than several days. Shafi'is and Hanbalis hold umrah obligatory once in a lifetime; Hanafis and Malikis call it a confirmed sunnah. Performing it in Ramadan is described in a well known hadith as equal in reward to a hajj, which does not remove the obligation of hajj itself.

short: The sanctified state a pilgrim enters with intention and talbiyah, marked by simple unsewn dress.
long: The root means to make something forbidden, because entering it makes ordinary permissible things off limits. Men wear two unsewn white cloths; women wear ordinary modest clothing with the face and hands uncovered, and there is no special ihram dress for them. The common misunderstanding is that the towels are the ihram; they are not, and a person who has made the intention is in ihram whatever they happen to be wearing.

short: The things forbidden while in ihram, such as perfume, cutting hair or nails, hunting and intimacy.
long: The Qur'an forbids sexual relations, wrongdoing and arguing during hajj, and forbids hunting land game while in ihram. To these are added perfume, cutting hair or nails, and for men sewn clothing and covering the head; most schools add contracting a marriage, which Hanafis permit. Breaking one out of forgetfulness is not sinful, though the schools differ over whether compensation is still owed, and doing it deliberately usually carries a dam or a fidyah of fasting, feeding or a sacrifice.

short: The fixed boundary points where a pilgrim must enter ihram before continuing towards Makkah.
long: The Prophet named four, one on each approach: Dhul Hulayfah for Madinah, al-Juhfah for Syria and Egypt, Qarn al-Manazil for Najd, and Yalamlam for Yemen. Dhat Irq, for those coming from Iraq, was fixed by Umar, and some report it from the Prophet as well. Anyone travelling through one, including passengers on a flight passing over it, enters ihram there or before. There is also a miqat in time: the months of hajj, Shawwal, Dhul Qa'dah and the first days of Dhul Hijjah.

short: The pilgrim's answering call, beginning labbayk Allahumma labbayk, here I am, my Lord, here I am.
long: It continues: no partner have You, here I am, all praise and favour are Yours, and the dominion, You have no partner. It is said on entering ihram and repeated on the road, aloud by men and quietly by women. It is an answer to the summons the Qur'an says Ibrahim was told to proclaim. On umrah pilgrims stop when they begin the tawaf; on hajj the talbiyah continues until the stoning on the tenth.

short: Circling the Kaaba seven times, keeping it on your left, starting and ending at the Black Stone.
long: The Qur'an commands circling the Ancient House. Most schools require the pilgrim to be in a state of purity, and Hanafis count a tawaf made without wudu as valid but owing a dam. Each circuit begins and ends at the corner of the Black Stone. Hajj has up to three: tawaf al-qudum on arrival, tawaf al-ifadah after Arafah which is a pillar of the hajj, and tawaf al-wada as a farewell before leaving Makkah. There is no obligation to touch or kiss the stone; most pilgrims simply point to it.

short: Walking seven times between the hills of Safa and Marwah, beginning at Safa and ending at Marwah.
long: It retraces Hajar's search for water for her infant son Isma'il, which ended with the spring of Zamzam. Each single crossing counts as one, so the seventh brings you to Marwah. The Qur'an names the two hills among the symbols of Allah. Men jog lightly between the two green markers, where the valley floor once lay; women walk throughout.

short: Standing at Arafah on the ninth of Dhul Hijjah, the one rite without which there is no hajj.
long: The Prophet said the hajj is Arafah. A pilgrim who reaches any part of the plain within its window has performed it, whether standing, sitting or asleep, and one who misses it has missed the hajj that year. The majority date the window from midday until dawn of the next day; Hanbalis start it at dawn on the ninth. The day is spent in supplication rather than in any set ritual.

short: The open plain east of Makkah where pilgrims gather on the ninth of Dhul Hijjah.
long: The small hill within it is called Jabal ar-Rahmah, the mount of mercy, and the farewell sermon was delivered nearby. Its day is the climax of the hajj. For Muslims not on hajj, fasting the day of Arafah is a strongly recommended sunnah described as expiating the year before and the year after; pilgrims themselves do not fast it.

short: The open ground between Arafah and Mina where pilgrims spend the night of the tenth.
long: The Qur'an calls it al-Mash'ar al-Haram, the Sacred Monument. Pilgrims arrive after sunset, pray Maghrib and Isha together, sleep on the ground under the sky, and gather pebbles for the stoning. The weak, the elderly and those accompanying them may move on to Mina in the later part of the night, a concession the Prophet gave to his own family.

short: The valley near Makkah where pilgrims camp before Arafah and for the days after Eid.
long: Pilgrims stay there on the eighth of Dhul Hijjah, called the day of tarwiyah, then return on the tenth after Arafah and remain for the days of tashriq, the eleventh to the thirteenth. The three jamarat stand at its edge. A pilgrim may leave after the twelfth if they depart before sunset; otherwise the thirteenth is completed.

short: The three pillars at Mina that pilgrims pelt with small pebbles, called ramy.
long: They mark the places where Ibrahim is said to have driven away the whisperer as he went to fulfil his command. On the tenth only the largest, Jamrat al-Aqabah, is stoned with seven pebbles; on the following days all three are stoned in order. The pebbles are the size of a chickpea, and the act is a symbol of refusal, not an attack on a physical devil. Those unable to go may appoint someone to stone on their behalf.

short: The animal offered in Makkah by pilgrims performing tamattu' or qiran, and its meat given away.
long: The word means a gift brought forward. It is a sheep or goat per pilgrim, or a seventh share of a camel or cow, slaughtered after the stoning on the tenth. The Qur'an says neither the meat nor the blood reaches Allah, only the God consciousness of the giver. It is different from the qurbani offered by Muslims everywhere at Eid, and different again from a dam owed as compensation.

short: Shaving the head after the rites, which releases the pilgrim from the state of ihram.
long: The Prophet asked mercy for those who shave three times and for those who trim once, so shaving is the better of the two for men. Women never shave; they gather their hair and cut about a fingertip's length from the end. It is done after the stoning on the tenth for hajj, and after the sa'i for umrah.

short: Trimming the hair rather than shaving it, the alternative way to leave ihram.
long: Most schools require a little to be taken from all around the head rather than a single snip from one place. It is the option chosen by women, and by men who wish to keep hair for a shave at the end of a hajj that follows soon after. Both halq and taqsir close the rites of umrah, and no further trimming is needed after that.

short: Coming out of ihram, so that what was forbidden during it becomes permitted again.
long: In hajj it happens in two stages. The first comes after stoning Jamrat al-Aqabah and cutting the hair: normal clothes and perfume return, but intimacy does not. The second comes after tawaf al-ifadah and its sa'i, and lifts everything. In umrah there is only one, after the hair is cut.

short: A compensating sacrifice owed for omitting a required rite of hajj or breaking a rule of ihram.
long: The word means blood. It is usually a sheep or goat, slaughtered in the sanctuary and given to the poor there, and for some breaches a person may instead fast or feed the needy. The schools differ over which acts are required rather than recommended, so an omission that costs a dam in one school may cost nothing in another. A dam repairs a shortfall; a hady is part of the pilgrimage itself.

short: One of the three ways to perform hajj: umrah first, then leaving ihram, then hajj from Makkah.
long: In tamattu' you complete umrah, come out of ihram and wait, then enter ihram again for hajj on the eighth. In qiran you hold both in a single unbroken ihram, and in ifrad you perform hajj alone. Tamattu' and qiran require a hady; ifrad does not. The schools differ over which is best, and tamattu' is what most pilgrims on organised trips perform.
